extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in Taiwanese politics, academic integrity, and the Li Mei-jhen case
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article describing the timeline, institutional responses, legal actions, and public commentary around a specific master's-thesis plagiarism controversy in Taiwan (Li Mei-jhen). It documents investigatory and policy standards invoked by universities and the Ministry of Education.

rubrics_metrics.name: University revocation procedure (announcement, recovery, removal)
rubrics_metrics.description: If plagiarism is confirmed and approved, an announcement of revocation will be posted on the university website, written notice will be issued to recover the degree certificate, and notifications will be sent to the National Central Library and the university library to remove both physical and digital copies of the thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the NSYSU-stated procedure for implementing degree revocation (explicit operational steps for publicizing and removing the awarded degree and the thesis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation must follow Degree Conferral Act
rubrics_metrics.description: The revocation of a degree is performed 'in accordance with the Degree Conferral Act.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal revocation actions are legally grounded and must follow the statutory procedures specified by the Degree Conferral Act (the university formally announced revocation under that law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for mandatory revocation (fabrication/alteration/plagiarism/ghostwriting/fraud)
rubrics_metrics.description: "If fabrication, alteration, plagiarism, ghostwriting, or other fraudulent conduct is confirmed, the degree must be revoked and the certificate publicly annulled."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ministry of Education policy language: these categories of academic misconduct are explicit triggers for mandatory revocation and public annulment of certificates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment standard: 'highly similar' / 'serious plagiarism' threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: University review committees used findings such as 'highly similar to others' works', 'serious plagiarism', or quantified similarity (e.g., '96% of the entire thesis had been plagiarized') as the basis for recommending revocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents both qualitative labels ('highly similar', 'serious') and quantitative claims (percent plagiarized) as evidentiary bases used in committee determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-stage review and expert consultation before action
rubrics_metrics.description: NSYSU convened a preliminary review committee, engaged external experts, and had internal review committees; the College of Social Sciences voted unanimously following reviews by three external experts and two internal review committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should (and in this case did) use multi-level review—including preliminary committee, external expert reviews, internal committees, and a college-level vote—before formally revoking a degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisors and examining committee accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Any supervising professors found to have been negligent would be reviewed by the Faculty Evaluation Committee; the Ministry and commentators stated that professors should be held responsible when students violate academic ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accountability extends beyond the student: advisors and oral-defense committee members can face investigation, review by teaching/faculty evaluation bodies, and administrative consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between voluntary 'relinquishment' and formal revocation by awarding institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that a student 'relinquishing' a degree is not equivalent to formal revocation—'only revocation by the awarding institution would be legitimate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal/ethical standing: voluntary giving up a degree does not replace the formal institutional revocation procedures and public record adjustments required under university/regulatory rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministry 'Li Mei-jhen Clause' reforms (mechanisms to strengthen thesis QA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ministry of Education introduced an eight-mechanism package (the 'Li Mei-jhen Clause') to strengthen quality assurance for university theses, including requiring advisors and departments to assume corresponding responsibility, reducing enrollment quotas as penalties, and planning development of a domestic thesis comparison system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This set of policy mechanisms is intended to make institutions and faculty more responsible for thesis quality and to provide systemic tools (e.g., a comparison system) and penalties to deter misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministry oversight/backstop if schools fail to act
rubrics_metrics.description: Director-General stated: 'If, after the Ministry’s requirements, schools still fail to improve or take action, the Ministry of Education will step in to handle the matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory backstop: the ministry can intervene when individual universities do not implement required improvements or enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality-control operational reforms (vet oral-defense lists; advisor-to-student ratios; alternative formats)
rubrics_metrics.description: NSYSU proposed reviewing the operation of in-service master's programs, strictly vetting oral defense committee lists, reviewing advisor-to-student ratios, and considering replacing research theses with technical reports for in-service and continuing-education programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of institutional-level reforms to reduce future plagiarism risk and improve oversight of graduate work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal consequences: potential criminal/copyright prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Qiaotou District Prosecutors Office indicted Li for violating the Copyright Act; commentators described plagiarism as potentially constituting criminal acts under copyright law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Academic misconduct can lead not only to academic penalties (revocation) but also to civil/criminal legal action under copyright statutes; institutions' findings may trigger prosecutorial investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational constraint: election bulletin printing deadlines limit credential changes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Kaohsiung City Election Commission stated that due to the large volume of printed election bulletins and their completion the following day, reprinting was not possible; the candidate applied to remove the wording 'Master's degree from National Sun Yat-sen University' from the election bulletin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing and administrative processes outside academia (election printing deadlines) can constrain how quickly credential information can be updated in public-facing materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of revoked-degree thesis copies from library collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon revocation, the university will notify the National Central Library and the university library to remove both physical and digital copies of the thesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revocation includes steps to remove the thesis from scholarly repositories and library holdings to reflect the annulled status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparative evidence and media/expert exposés as triggers for investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The controversy began with media and whistleblower comparisons (e.g., Mirror Weekly finding 96% similarity) exposing verbatim copying, which prompted the university's investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicly produced comparative analyses and whistleblower evidence can prompt formal institutional reviews even years after degree conferral.
